conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, thanks. I’ve been having this abdominal pain again—same kind as my old pancreatitis episodes. It started about a week ago with nausea, then the pain came back in the middle and right side, going through to my back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Was it as severe as your last pancreatitis episode?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not quite as bad, but still pretty uncomfortable. I had a CT scan six days ago—my doctor said there might be some inflammation in the tail of my pancreas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I reviewed that. It showed a slightly bulky tail but no clear signs of active pancreatitis. We’ll need to look deeper. You mentioned you left the hospital yesterday after getting orange juice and vomiting—why did you come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just wasn’t getting better. The nausea kept coming back, and I felt weak. I knew I needed more help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That was the right call. We’re going to keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—for now, give you IV fluids, and control your pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will I be able to eat soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start slow. Once your symptoms settle, we’ll try clear liquids. It might take a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ve also been feeling a bit feverish—temperature up to 100.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw that. Your urine test showed some signs of infection—moderate bacteria and white cells—so we started you on Levaquin for a UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I’ve had UTIs before. I’ve also been having trouble emptying my bladder sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be contributing. We’ll treat the infection and monitor. We also checked your blood work—your hemoglobin has been dropping a bit, so we’re watching for anemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had iron deficiency before. Is that related to the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Given your history of malabsorption and Sjogren’s, we’re concerned there might be an issue in your small intestine. We’re planning an EGD and capsule endoscopy to look inside.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s a capsule endoscopy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You swallow a small pill-sized camera that takes pictures as it moves through your gut. It helps us see the small bowel, which we can’t reach with regular scopes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds interesting. When will that happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Early next week. First, we need you stable and hydrated. We also did an ultrasound today to check your gallbladder—everything looked normal, so it’s not gallstones causing this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. My mom had her gallbladder out—always worried I’d get it too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. Nausea is less, but I still have some pain in the upper right side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning show your kidney function is good, and your amylase and lipase are normal—so no active pancreatitis. But your potassium is a bit low at 3.1, so we’re giving you some supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had low potassium before—especially when I was on full-dose Florinef. I’m on half now, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we kept it at half-dose because of that. Your blood pressure has been on the lower side—around 95 systolic—so we held your Betaxolol for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t felt dizzy, but I know I’d get more tachycardic if I stood up for long.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep monitoring. For now, we’re going to try advancing your diet to clear liquids if you’re up for it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please. I’m tired of just IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well with clear liquids yesterday. Today, we’re giving you toast. How’s your stomach holding up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I had the whole piece and no vomiting. Pain is still there but milder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re switching your pain meds from IV to oral Dilaudid. You can take it every few hours as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I’d rather not be on IVs anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we did your EGD and capsule endoscopy. The upper endoscopy didn’t show anything obvious, but we took biopsies from your duodenum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What did they find?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The biopsies show chronic duodenitis—ongoing inflammation. It could be from celiac disease, Crohn’s, or another form of IBD. We’re sending more tests to figure it out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a sigmoidoscopy years ago that showed inflammation. Could this be Crohn’s?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible. That’s why we tried to do a colonoscopy—to look at the rest of your colon. But even after your prep, there was still too much stool.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I thought I cleared out. What happens now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need to come back and do a two-day GoLytely prep to clean things out fully. Then we can get a clear view.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. You’ve been on solids, no vomiting, pain is much better. We’re thinking about discharge in a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What will I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue advancing your diet slowly. Stay on the omeprazole we started—it helps with gut inflammation. And take the Creon with meals; it helps with digestion since you have malabsorption.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve taken Creon before. How long should I stay on it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, indefinitely. We’ll reassess once we get all your biopsy results and complete the colonoscopy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your UTI treatment is complete—three days of Levaquin. No more fevers, and your symptoms have improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. My bladder feels normal now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re clearing you for discharge today. You’re tolerating food, pain is minimal, and you don’t need IV meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need to schedule the colonoscopy with a full prep. We’re also adding Midodrine for your orthostatic symptoms, and we lowered your Betaxolol dose to 10mg to keep your heart rate stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue amitriptyline for sleep, Lexapro for mood, and Florinef at 0.2mg twice daily. Take the hydromorphone only if pain flares up, and don’t hesitate to come back if you can’t keep liquids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I’m glad I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did the right thing. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you’ve been having abdominal pain since your test today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started during the MRCP when they gave me that secretin shot. It was sharp, right here in the upper belly, but only lasted a few minutes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And then it came back later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: About two hours after I got home. It got worse—radiated to my back, with nausea. I took my usual Dilaudid, but it didn’t help much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds like a flare of pancreatitis, especially given your history. We’ll keep you NPO for now—nothing by mouth—to let your pancreas rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? But the pain was only brief during the test. Is this really pancreatitis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, secretin can trigger it, even if the test itself is safe for most. Your symptoms are classic—epigastric pain, nausea, radiation to the back. We’ve started IV fluids and will give you IV pain meds to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My lipase was only 40 in the ER—is that high enough?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s on the lower side, but we don’t always see big enzyme rises, especially with mild or early episodes. Your history and symptoms guide us more here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How’s the pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. The IV meds helped. I’m not nauseous anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll start you on clear liquids tomorrow if you stay comfortable. We also reviewed your MRCP—no changes in the cysts, and your pancreatic duct responded normally to secretin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are the cysts still there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but they’re small and unchanged—8 mm and under, no signs of concern. The biliary irregularities we saw before are also less noticeable, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well overnight. You’re pain-free and tolerating sips. We’ll advance you to a soft diet and get ready for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my other meds? I take Creon, omeprazole, and the ones for my blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue all of them. We’re adjusting your fludrocortisone to half dose—0.1 mg twice daily—because you tend to get low potassium. Midodrine you’ll restart at home when you’re up and moving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my antidepressant and amitriptyline?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, both continue. We lowered amitriptyline to 25 mg at night to help with side effects, but it’s still important for sleep and nerve-related pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable, and you’ve eaten without pain. We’re clearing you to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Avoid fatty and high-protein foods for a few days. Reintroduce them slowly. If you develop fever, chills, or vomiting, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll schedule a visit with your gastroenterologist to review the MRCP and your pancreatitis history. Keep taking Creon with all meals—six capsules now, as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m glad it wasn’t worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You responded well. Just take it easy the next few days, stay hydrated, and follow the diet plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge papers are ready. You’re cleared to leave whenever you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate all the help. I’ll follow up as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were brought in by EMS for abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. The pain started in my upper belly, mostly on the left side, and it’s been coming and going since I got home from the hospital last week. But last night, it became constant and really intense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Did you have any nausea, vomiting, or fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nausea, yes, and chills, but no fever or vomiting. I’ve also been really constipated since I’ve been taking Dilaudid at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You mentioned you were in the ER a few days ago after a fall. Was that related to this pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I think I passed out from the pain at work. I hit my side and had blood in my urine, but the CT scan didn’t show any serious injury.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right, I reviewed that. The CT head and abdomen were both negative for bleeding or hematoma. We’ll keep an eye on that, but it seems stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history of pancreatitis, especially after the MRCP with secretin last time, we’re concerned this could be another flare-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. The pain feels similar—deep in the upper belly, not really moving around.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your blood work. Your lipase was 43 when you arrived, which is only slightly elevated. That’s lower than a typical pancreatitis flare, but we’re not ruling it out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So is it pancreatitis or not?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible, but your symptoms and exam also suggest the pain could be from severe constipation. Your belly is soft, and you don’t have guarding or rebound tenderness, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had a bowel movement in three days. That’s not normal for me, even with pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We ordered an X-ray of your abdomen to check for stool burden. We’ll use that to guide treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your abdominal X-ray is back. It shows a lot of stool throughout your colon, which explains part of your discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, so it’s mostly constipation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s a combination—your chronic pancreatitis may be flaring slightly, but the constipation is definitely making it worse. We’re going to start a bowel regimen to help clear things out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What will that involve?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you a dose of polyethylene glycol today, followed by senna twice daily. We’ll also keep you on IV fluids and hold solid food for now to rest your pancreas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds reasonable. I’ve been on Dilaudid, but it hasn’t helped much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we avoided morphine because you’re allergic, and Dilaudid can worsen constipation. We’re using it sparingly and adding acetaminophen for better pain control with fewer side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You passed a lot of stool overnight, and you’re reporting less pain. That’s a great sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the pressure in my belly is much better. I still have some dull ache, but it’s manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs this morning show your lipase dropped to 18, which is normal. Liver enzymes and kidney function are also stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the pancreatitis is resolving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks like it was a mild episode, if present at all. The improvement after bowel treatment suggests constipation was the main driver this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad to hear that. What about my other labs? I’ve been anemic before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin dropped from 12.7 to 10.3, so you’re more anemic than before. But it’s been a chronic issue, and there’s no sign of acute bleeding. We’ll continue monitoring it as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. And my POTS and Sjogren’s—should I keep taking my usual meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve continued your fludrocortisone, betaxolol, and omeprazole. We held midodrine this admission since you preferred it last time, but we can restart if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I’d rather not. It makes me feel jittery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. We’ll keep focusing on volume support with fluids and fludrocortisone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had no pain overnight, and you tolerated sipping clear liquids well. We’re going to advance you to a soft diet today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great! Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re getting close. We want to make sure you can eat without pain and that your bowel movements stay regular.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had two soft stools today, and no nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We also got your stool test back—no C. diff toxin, so we don’t need antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. What about the urine culture from the ER?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That showed mixed bacteria, but it’s consistent with contamination, not infection. No treatment needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had two full days with minimal pain, normal labs, and regular bowel movements. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news. What should I do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send you home with senna as needed for constipation, acetaminophen for pain, and a short course of Dilaudid for breakthrough pain—only 10 days’ supply.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my enzyme supplements? I usually take six capsules with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re reducing that to one capsule four times a day. Your malabsorption is stable, and high doses can sometimes irritate the pancreas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that. Should I follow up with my gastroenterologist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, Dr. Chen will see you in two weeks. Also, keep taking your folic acid, amitriptyline, and escitalopram as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been anxious about these pain episodes. It’s hard to predict when they’ll happen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Try to identify triggers—like certain foods or stress. Stay hydrated, manage constipation early, and don’t hesitate to call your doctor if pain worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your discharge labs are stable, and you’ve eaten breakfast without issues. We’re clearing you to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: call your primary care provider with any concerns, and go to the ER if you develop a fever over 101, severe pain, or can’t keep food down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll schedule my follow-up today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, and we hope you stay comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the surgical team. You're here because of recurrent pancreatitis and a cyst in the tail of your pancreas. We’re planning to do a distal pancreatectomy and remove the spleen today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes, I’ve been having a lot of left-sided pain. Is the surgery definitely needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ve had multiple episodes of pancreatitis with no clear cause. Imaging shows the body and tail of the pancreas are enlarged, and the pain is centered there. Removing that part should help prevent future attacks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the spleen too? Why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because the blood supply to the spleen comes from the same artery that runs through the tail of the pancreas. It’s safer to remove it during this surgery to avoid complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m also worried about my digestion. I’ve had malabsorption for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s why we’re also doing a small bowel biopsy. We’ll take a small sample to check if there’s any underlying issue causing the malabsorption.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need lifelong supplements after this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Since part of the pancreas is being removed, you may need pancreatic enzyme supplements. We’ll monitor that closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my anemia? That’s been a problem too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your hemoglobin is low. We’ll keep an eye on it. The surgery team will be cautious due to your Von Willebrand’s disease, which affects clotting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m also allergic to morphine. I get really nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. We’ll use alternative pain medications. You’ll have a PCA pump initially, but not with morphine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, we just got back from surgery. The distal pancreatectomy and splenectomy went well. We also did the small bowel biopsy. You’re in recovery now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How do I feel? I’m groggy but okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. You’ll be on IV fluids and pain meds. You’re not allowed to eat yet—NPO—until your bowels wake up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will that take?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Usually a few days. We’ll start with clear liquids once you pass gas and your abdomen isn’t bloated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your NG tube was removed this morning. That’s a good sign—your stomach is starting to work again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That feels better. Can I drink water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We’ll wait until you have bowel sounds and some flatus. Maybe tomorrow for sips.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. WBC was high yesterday but is coming down. That’s expected after surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the infection risk higher without a spleen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, long-term. You’ll need vaccines and to be careful with fevers. But for now, you’re on antibiotics just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—you passed gas and your abdomen is soft. We’re going to start you on clear liquids today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have apple juice?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, small amounts. We’ll watch for nausea or bloating. If you tolerate it, we’ll advance your diet slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your pain is better, and you’re on oral pain meds now. We’re switching from the PCA pump.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still need a higher dose than usual, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ve always needed more. We’re using a combination to keep you comfortable without over-sedation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the biopsy results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The small bowel biopsy came back normal. No signs of celiac or other malabsorption causes. That’s good—we can focus on pancreatic support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your JP drain amylase was checked yesterday—117. That’s a bit elevated, but not concerning. We’ll remove the drain today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What does that number mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It checks for pancreatic fluid leak. A high level could mean a leak, but yours isn’t high enough to worry. You’re healing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pancreas tissue they removed—was there pancreatitis or a cyst?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Actually, no. The pathology report says the tissue looked normal—no cyst, no signs of chronic pancreatitis. But that doesn’t mean the surgery wasn’t needed. Sometimes damage isn’t visible under the microscope.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why did I keep having attacks?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t know for sure. It could be functional or due to subtle structural issues. But since your pain was localized there, removing it was the best option.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling a bit dizzy when I sit up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely your orthostatic hypotension. You have a history of that. We’re monitoring your blood pressure and restarted your fludrocortisone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart racing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also part of your condition. You have tachycardia syndrome. As long as you’re not symptomatic, it’s okay. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. You’ve had a bowel movement, you’re on a regular diet, and your incision looks clean. We’re discharging you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy for a few weeks. No heavy lifting. Keep the steri strips on until they fall off. Watch for fever, redness, or drainage from the incision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were brought in from the ED with abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes. I was discharged just a few days ago, and I felt okay that night, but the next morning the pain came back—same as before. It’s in my upper belly, goes to my back, and gets worse after eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds like your typical flare. You mentioned nausea and vomiting too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I haven’t been able to keep anything down. And last night, I threw up and there was a little blood—maybe a tablespoon. It happened again this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. The team noted that—called hematemesis. Given your history of wretching, it’s likely a small tear in the esophagus. Your blood count is stable, so that’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? I was worried it might be something worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can happen with forceful vomiting. You had an EGD three weeks ago, and it showed mild esophagitis but no ulcers or bleeding sites. So we think this is related to the vomiting, not a new bleed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. But why is this pain happening so often now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we’re trying to figure out. You have chronic pancreatitis, which we believe may be linked to your underlying autoimmune issues like Sjogren’s and possible vasculitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’m on methotrexate for that. Shouldn’t that be helping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should, and it has helped with your malabsorption. But your pain flares keep recurring. We’ve consulted rheumatology to see if your vasculitis might be active.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what did they say?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They reviewed your case and don’t think you’re having an active vasculitis flare right now. But we’re waiting on some blood tests—like anti-Ro/La, RNP, and cryoglobulins—to be sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my pancreas? Could this be another pancreatitis attack?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your lipase and amylase—both are normal. Your ultrasound also didn’t show any gallstones or duct blockages. The pancreas that’s left looks normal.

conversation_lines.text: So if it’s not pancreatitis, what is causing the pain?

conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.text: Hi, thanks. I’ve been having really bad stomach pain again—same kind I’ve had before with pancreatitis. It started last night after my boyfriend’s birthday party. I ate some fatty food, and then the pain just hit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds consistent with your past flares. Was this pain different in any way?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, actually. I’ve had these weird episodes—like crampy pain all over my belly, not just the usual spot. It comes and goes, lasts a few minutes, and I feel dizzy, like I might pass out. That’s new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. Any fever or other symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had a low-grade fever—100.1—and a mild headache. No cough or sore throat. Oh, and I noticed a rash on my right arm yesterday. It looks kind of like the vasculitis rashes I’ve had before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’ll check that out. You’re on methotrexate for your vasculitis—any recent changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, same dose. But I did get a portacath placed five days ago—on the left side. It went fine, no issues since.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good to know. We’ll keep an eye on it. For now, we’re going to keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—to let your pancreas rest. We’ll give you IV fluids and pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. The nausea’s better since the Zofran in the ER, but the pain’s still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll adjust your pain meds. You got IV Dilaudid earlier—we’ll continue that as needed. We also checked labs—your white count is a bit high, but amylase is normal. Still, given your history, we’re treating this as acute on chronic pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Wait, amylase is normal? I thought that’s always high with pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. In chronic pancreatitis, especially with repeated flares, the pancreas may not produce as much enzyme, so amylase can be normal. We rely on your symptoms and history too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. What about the dizziness and cramps? Should we be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring that. Your blood pressure and heart rate show some orthostatic changes, which fits with your POTS. We’ll keep you on your usual meds—midodrine, florinef, betaxolol—to help stabilize it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Morning. The pain’s a little better, but I still can’t eat. The dizziness episodes are less frequent, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. Your labs are stable. We’re going to keep you NPO for now, but we’ll try advancing to clear liquids later if you’re still improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about the rash? It hasn’t changed much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We looked at it—the skin is warm but no ulceration. Given your history, we’re watching it closely, but it doesn’t look like active vasculitis. We’ll hold off on steroids for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my methotrexate? I’m due for my weekly shot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll give it today. Your rheumatologist wants to increase the dose slightly to help control inflammation long-term, but we’ll do that after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to try you on clear liquids now—start with broth and see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great, I’m ready to try. Any chance I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We need to make sure you can keep food down and that your pain is controlled with oral meds. We’ll reassess tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You tolerated the clear liquids well. We’re advancing you to a soft diet—low fat, small meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. My pain is much better—only taking the hydromorphone once last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’re also switching you from IV to oral pain meds to make sure they work. Your dizziness hasn’t returned, which is great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my other meds? Can I restart them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve restarted your hydroxychloroquine, pantoprazole, and the others. We’re adjusting your antidepressants—lowering the escitalopram and amitriptyline slightly to reduce side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been worried—do you think this flare was just from stress and food, or is something else going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely, yes—stress and fatty foods are common triggers for you. The rheumatology workup was negative this time, so no sign of active vasculitis driving it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. We think you’re ready to go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep an eye on your pain—if it gets worse or different, or if you can’t keep food down, come back. Also, if the dizziness returns or the rash spreads.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diet? I don’t want to trigger another flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Start slow—low-fat, small meals. Use your pancreatic enzymes with every meal. Avoid alcohol and greasy foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge. We’re giving you updated prescriptions, including Protonix instead of pantoprazole, and adjusted doses for your other meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll follow up with my doctors and take it easy with midterms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Manage stress, stick to your meds, and call if anything changes. You’re doing well—let’s keep it that way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be helping take care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, thanks. I’ve been having abdominal pain again—started in my right upper side, but now it’s moved to the middle, under my ribs. It’s been getting worse, especially with eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any nausea or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a lot. I’ve been vomiting bile, and one time there was a little blood in it. I haven’t been able to keep anything down—food or even my pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And the pain—does it feel like your usual pancreatitis episodes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: At first it was different, in the right side, but now it’s back to the epigastric pain I usually get. I also had a gray-colored stool, which worries me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. We’ll run some tests, but this does sound consistent with a flare of your chronic pancreatitis, possibly related to your vasculitis. We’ll keep you NPO for now—no food or drink by mouth—to let your pancreas rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. But I was doing okay after my last hospitalization. I even went back to school and work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s frustrating. These flares can come on even when you’re feeling better. We’re giving you IV fluids and starting IV Dilaudid for pain. We also gave you Zofran for nausea in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. The pain’s still pretty bad, but the meds helped a little earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs came back. Your lipase is only slightly elevated at 32, which is unusual for acute pancreatitis, but given your history, we’re still treating this as a flare. Your kidney function is good, and no signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not pancreatitis then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could still be. In chronic cases like yours, the lipase doesn’t always spike. Your symptoms and history are very consistent. We’re also watching for complications, but so far, you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. I was worried something else was going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an abdominal X-ray. It shows a lot of stool in your colon, but no blockage. Given your history of malabsorption and chronic pancreatitis, this isn’t uncommon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could that be making the pain worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Constipation can aggravate abdominal discomfort, especially with your condition. We’ll monitor it, but right now, the priority is controlling your pain and letting your gut rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling this morning? Any nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still nauseous. I tried to sip water last night but threw it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, we’ll keep you NPO a bit longer. We’re continuing IV fluids and adjusting your pain meds. We’re also holding off on oral meds until you can keep them down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my methotrexate? I just started it last month.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re aware. You’ll get your weekly injection tomorrow, as scheduled. It’s important for controlling your underlying vasculitis and may help reduce future flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture came back. It showed lactobacillus, which is a normal bacterium, not an infection. So no antibiotics needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. I was worried about a UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re looking better. Your heart rate has come down, and you say the nausea is improving. Want to try a small sip of water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’d like to try. I haven’t had anything in days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll start with ice chips and clear liquids. If you keep that down, we can advance your diet slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You kept the ice chips and broth down. How’s your stomach feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Still some dull pain, but not nauseous anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. We’re going to try giving your oral meds again—your Dilaudid, Zofran, and the others. Start with one pill and see how it goes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try. I really need my pain meds by mouth so I can get off the IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You kept the pills down! We’re switching you to oral Dilaudid and Tylenol for pain. You’re also getting your methotrexate injection today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried I’d have to stay longer if I couldn’t take pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’ll keep advancing your diet—maybe some toast or crackers today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You ate a full meal yesterday and kept it down. How’s the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I only took one Dilaudid last night. I think I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re close. We want to make sure you can manage your pain and keep food down for another full day. We’ll also go over your discharge meds and plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I still take the same medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mostly yes. We’re adjusting your Amitriptyline to 50 mg at bedtime for better pain and sleep support. Your Dilaudid dose is lower—2 mg as needed—and we’re adding Docusate and Senna to prevent constipation from the opioids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, and my enzyme supplements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll take five pancreatic enzyme capsules with each meal and snacks. That helps with digestion and malabsorption.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs today look good. Kidney function is excellent, bicarbonate is up, and no anemia. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning if you continue to do well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news! What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or come back if you have worsening pain, fevers, vomiting, or lightheadedness. Also, keep taking your midodrine and fludrocortisone for POTS—your heart rate was still jumping when you stood up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know—my heart races when I stand. But it’s been better since I’ve been lying down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made it through the night with no vomiting and good pain control. We’re clearing you for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I’m really glad I can go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep up with your methotrexate, enzymes, and follow-up with your rheumatologist and GI doctor. Take it slow with eating—avoid fatty foods that can trigger flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve learned my lesson about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send all your discharge instructions and meds with you. Feel better, and take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, Dr. Lee. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it all. Meds, diet, warning signs. I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’re glad you’re feeling better. Take care and follow up as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in with your discharge paperwork and prescriptions shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m gathering my things now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check—vitals are stable, you’ve eaten lunch, and you’re still doing well. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great! I’m so ready to be home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad we could help. Remember to rest, stay hydrated, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for all your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care and get some rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I definitely will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Bye!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, thanks for coming. I’ve been having really bad stomach pain again—same as before, in the middle, radiating to my back. And yesterday, after vomiting for a few minutes, I threw up blood—bright red and some clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. That sounds scary. Was this after eating something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I had a grilled cheese sandwich the day before, and my pain got worse. Then at school, I felt nauseous, ate a granola bar, and started vomiting. That’s when the blood came.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that helps. Given your history of pancreatitis and vasculitis, this could be a flare. The vomiting blood might be from a small tear in your esophagus—called a Mallory-Weiss tear—especially since it happened after prolonged vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I’ve had those before. But I’m worried—how bad is the bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hematocrit was 27.1 when you arrived, which is low but stable. It hasn’t dropped further, and you’re not feeling lightheaded or short of breath, so we don’t think you’re actively bleeding now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. But the pain is still pretty bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—for now to let your pancreas rest. We’ll give you IV fluids and pain medication through your IV. You’ll get Dilaudid for pain and Zofran for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my other meds—like for POTS and Sjogren’s—will I get those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll hold the oral meds until you can tolerate sips. But once you can, we’ll restart them. For now, we’re continuing your fludrocortisone and midodrine for POTS. Betaxolol is paused because your blood pressure was a bit low earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, right. I did feel dizzy after my last dose. Is that why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely. You have low baseline BP, and Betaxolol can drop it further. We gave you a fluid bolus, and your pressure improved. We’ll restart it later if needed, maybe at a lower dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling? Pain under control?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. Still nauseous, but the pain’s not as sharp. Did the blood come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had another small episode of hematemesis last night, but your hematocrit stayed stable at 26.3. We’re keeping you on IV pantoprazole to reduce stomach acid and help the tear heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. When can I try drinking something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll try small sips of water later today if your nausea stays under control. No food yet. We’re also watching your labs—your kidney function and electrolytes look good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You made it through the night without vomiting. That’s great. We’re going to start you on clear liquids—water, broth, apple juice. Try small amounts every hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s good news. Can I have ginger ale?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, flat ginger ale is fine. And we’re switching your pain meds to oral Dilaudid since you can take pills. We’ll keep the IV as backup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my enzymes? I know I need them with any food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We’ll restart your pancreatic enzymes when you move to full liquids. For now, just focus on keeping the clear liquids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve tolerated clear liquids well. Today, we’re advancing you to full liquids—yogurt, pudding, cream of wheat. How’s your constipation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still no bowel movement. I’m on opioids, so that’s not surprising.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you a Bisacodyl suppository yesterday—you had a few bowel movements, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, twice. But I’d like something I can take by mouth going forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll add senna to your discharge meds for that. And keep docusate. We want to prevent constipation, especially with pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my methotrexate? I usually get it weekly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get your methotrexate injection tomorrow. Your rheumatology team is considering increasing the dose to better control your vasculitis flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. No more vomiting or blood. We’re starting you on a bland diet—soft foods like mashed potatoes, toast, applesauce.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great! Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you tolerate meals today and tomorrow, yes. We’ll monitor you for one full day on solids before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds—will they change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A few adjustments. We’re lowering fludrocortisone to 0.1 mg twice daily. Escitalopram is reduced to 10 mg daily due to your anxiety improvement. Betaxolol is now as-needed for POTS symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the Dilaudid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have a prescription for oral hydromorphone as needed. But try to use acetaminophen first to minimize opioid use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a good day yesterday—three full meals, no nausea. We’re planning discharge tomorrow if today goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Should I expect another flare soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can’t prevent all flares, but your team is working on adjusting methotrexate and prednisone to reduce frequency. Avoid fatty foods—like grilled cheese—for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Definitely. I learned my lesson. What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your GI and rheumatology teams next week. They’ll review your flare and adjust long-term treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Another good day. You’re officially discharge-ready. We’ll finalize your instructions and send you home this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. Just to confirm—I stay on full liquids tomorrow, then bland diet for two weeks?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Small, frequent meals. No alcohol, no fatty or spicy foods. And take your pancreatic enzymes with every meal—five capsules now, up from five before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the pantoprazole—why am I starting that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: To help prevent another esophageal tear. We’ll keep it for a few weeks to let the area heal fully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. And if I vomit blood again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Go to the ER. Same for severe pain, chest pain, or dizziness. Otherwise, call your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I feel much better. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad you’re improving. Nurse will go over your meds and diet one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check-in. Any pain or nausea overnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: None. Slept well. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll discharge you later today. Keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. Your discharge papers are ready. You’re stable, pain is controlled, and you’re tolerating food well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll follow the diet and meds closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And remember—call if you have any concerns. It was good taking care of you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. See you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve already started two liters of normal saline. You were dehydrated. We’ll continue that and give you IV Dilaudid for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. And my methotrexate? I was supposed to get it this week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you your 25mg dose by injection while you’re here. Your rheumatologist wants to keep you on it—it’s been helping your vasculitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve noticed my digestion has been better since starting it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable—no infection in blood or urine. We did an ultrasound yesterday—gallbladder looks fine, no stones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Was the pancreas clear?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s hard to see due to bowel gas, but there’s no fluid around it, which is reassuring. We didn’t do a CT because your exam hasn’t changed much from past scans.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d rather avoid another CT if we can. So what now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on IV fluids and pain meds. If your pain improves, we’ll start you on clear liquids tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing better. Pain is down, and you haven’t vomited since yesterday. We’re going to try clear liquids—apple juice, broth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Can I have ginger ale?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as long as it’s flat. We’ll watch for nausea. Also, we restarted your amitriptyline and escitalopram this morning—they were held while you were NPO.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling anxious. Glad to have those back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You tolerated the clear liquids well. We’re advancing you to full liquids—yogurt, pudding, cream of wheat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have mashed potatoes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Soon. Let’s stick to smooth foods for now. We want to avoid stressing your pancreas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Urine culture came back—no significant growth. So no UTI. That’s good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the rash I had in the ER? It’s gone now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely related to your vasculitis or a viral reaction. Since it’s resolved and no other signs, we’re not worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had a bowel movement in days. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, and with your opioid use, constipation is a concern. We’ll keep you on docusate and senna.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. Pain is mild, you’re eating soft foods, and you’re more mobile. We’re going to switch you to oral pain meds—Dilaudid by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d prefer that. IVs are uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re planning your discharge for tomorrow. You’re tolerating a bland diet, pain is controlled, and you’re walking without dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re increasing your escitalopram to 20mg at night for anxiety. Pantoprazole will be twice daily to protect your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And betaxolol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re increasing it to 20mg daily for POTS. You’ll get a prescription for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using midodrine at home, but it gives me headaches lying down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s why we didn’t restart it here. Fludrocortisone and betaxolol should help enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried if the fever comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Also watch for worsening pain, vomiting, or dizziness. If any of those happen, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my weight loss—15 pounds. Should I see a dietitian?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good idea. We’ll refer you. Your malabsorption has improved, but nutrition is key with chronic pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home today. You’re stable, walking, and eating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll follow up with rheumatology and GI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your primary doctor too. Keep taking your enzymes with meals—they help digestion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t forget. And I’ll get my methotrexate injection on schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll send all prescriptions to your pharmacy. Take it easy at home, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Get some rest and stay hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. The fatigue has been real.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s been a tough few days. Give yourself time to recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll avoid heavy meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Smart. Stick to small, low-fat meals. Your pancreas will thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. No fried food, no big portions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And keep up with your bowel regimen—don’t let constipation sneak up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll take my senna every morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. We’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring your discharge papers shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll wait for them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you back to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, thanks for coming. I just got discharged a couple days ago, but last night I ate a quarter of a sandwich and everything came back—severe pain, nausea, vomiting, fevers, chills.

conversation_lines.text: I see. Where’s the pain located?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same as before—epigastric and right upper quadrant. It hasn’t changed in months. I couldn’t even walk to my clinic, so I went to the ER instead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds really tough. Any pain meds since then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I got some relief at the other hospital, but nothing in the last few hours. It’s getting worse again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, we’ll get you some IV Dilaudid to help with that. You mentioned vomiting—have you kept anything down today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’ll start with IV meds and fluids for now. You’re on Zofran at home—want us to give that IV?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please. And I haven’t had a bowel movement in two days. I can’t take my stool softeners by mouth. Can I get a suppository tomorrow morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We can give a Dulcolax suppository in the morning. Let’s focus on getting your nausea and pain under control first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pain med should be kicking in soon. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better, thank you. The sharpness is gone, but it’s still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We reviewed your imaging from earlier today. The CT scan shows no signs of pancreatitis or kidney stones. Your gallbladder looks normal too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not pancreatitis again? But the pain feels just like the flares I’ve had before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The scan doesn’t show active inflammation. But we know your chronic pain is real. It’s possible this is a flare of your chronic pancreatitis, even if it’s not showing up on imaging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve lost about 20 pounds since this all started. I’m worried I’m not getting enough nutrition. Should I be on TPN?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your albumin level—it’s normal at 3.8. That suggests your protein stores are okay for now. We don’t think TPN is needed, but we can connect you with a dietitian to talk about nutritional support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d really appreciate that. I’m trying to keep up with school, but missing classes is hard—even if I still have straight A’s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great managing all this. We’ll make sure you’re stable before discharge. Now, about your methotrexate—your PCP is continuing it weekly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 25 mg weekly. I was supposed to see my doctor today to talk about increasing the dose, but I missed the appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We confirmed with their office. We’ll give you the methotrexate injection tonight. But the skin biopsy didn’t show vasculitis—so we’re not entirely sure what’s driving the inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So is it still helping? I feel like I need something to keep this under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It may still be helping your malabsorption, which has improved. But we’re not seeing clear evidence of active vasculitis. Your PCP will help decide if the dose should go up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s your pain and nausea today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I haven’t vomited since last night. I might be able to try some liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll start you on clear liquids—water, broth, apple juice. If you keep that down, we’ll advance to full liquids, then regular food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my constipation? I had the suppository this morning and had a bowel movement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We’ll switch to oral Senna and add bisacodyl as needed. Avoid narcotics when possible—they make it worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know, but the pain is so bad sometimes I have to take the Dilaudid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. We’re balancing pain control with side effects. Your POTS is stable—we’re continuing fludrocortisone and betaxolol as usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want another syncopal episode. I’m just frustrated—this keeps happening, and I don’t feel like anyone is coordinating my care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. We’ll make sure your PCP and specialists are updated. You’re seeing Dr. ___ soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not for a few weeks. I wish it were sooner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll flag that for your team. For now, focus on advancing your diet and staying hydrated. You’re making good progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well—tolerated full liquids, now moving to a regular diet. How’s the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I had a small meal and felt okay. Still some discomfort, but manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning if this continues. No new medications—just your usual ones with a few adjustments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Adjustments? I thought I was going home on the same meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re lowering your escitalopram and betaxolol doses slightly—based on how you’re doing. You’ll take 10 mg escitalopram and 10 mg betaxolol daily. The rest stays the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s fine. And I’ll follow up with my doctors?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your PCP and specialists are aware. Try to keep those appointments—they’re important for managing your chronic conditions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made it through the night with no issues. We’ll discharge you in an hour or so. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just one—should I worry about the weight loss? I still feel like I’m not eating enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your albumin is normal, which is reassuring. Keep working with your care team on nutrition. Maybe ask your PCP for a dietitian referral.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And thank you—for listening. It means a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi. I’ve been having that same abdominal pain again—epigastric, radiating to my back. It’s worse after eating. And I threw up blood this morning.

conversation_lines.text: I see. That’s concerning. Was it bright red or dark? Any black stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bright red with some black flecks. No diarrhea, but I’ve been nauseous for days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’re going to keep you NPO for now, start IV fluids, and give you some anti-nausea and pain meds. We also need to check on the bleeding.

conversation_lines.text: I’ve had this before. They said it might be from vomiting so much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does this keep happening? I’m scared I’m going to bleed again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you an IV medication called a PPI to reduce stomach acid and help any small tear heal. We’ll monitor your blood count closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. But the pain—it’s so severe. Is it my pancreas again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed your imaging and labs. Your lipase is normal, and past scans don’t show chronic pancreatitis. Your pancreatologist doesn’t think this is pancreatic pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’ve had over 40 admissions for this. What else could it be?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re looking into other causes. Rheumatology was consulted because you’ve been on methotrexate. But they don’t see clear evidence of vasculitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But my doctor started it because I felt better on it. Does that not matter?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your response is important, but we need to balance risks. Without a confirmed diagnosis, long-term immunosuppression isn’t recommended. We’re stopping methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s scary. What if the pain gets worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not stopping pain control. You’ll still get IV meds as needed. But we’re trying to find a long-term plan that doesn’t rely only on hospital visits.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want to feel normal. I’ve lost weight and can’t eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. Nutrition is a concern. We sent a pre-albumin level, but it’s pending. For now, you’re getting IV fluids with dextrose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my Sjogren’s? Could that be causing this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my amitriptyline? I take it for sleep and palpitations.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to taper it down. Tricyclics like amitriptyline can slow gut motility and make nausea worse. We’ll reduce it over the next few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I need it to sleep. What will I do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll work with your psychiatrist on alternatives. Your escitalopram dose is being cut in half too, so mental health support is key.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. Still nauseous, but the pain is less sharp.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Your hemoglobin stabilized. The drop was likely from fluid overload and not major bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I didn’t need that blood transfusion after all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did get one unit at the other hospital, but your current levels are consistent with chronic anemia, possibly from iron deficiency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What happens now? Can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’d like to keep you a bit longer to see if you can tolerate liquids. But we understand you want to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do. I’m tired of being here. But I don’t want to come back in two days.
