conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds helpful. What else should I do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We recommend seeing your primary doctor soon, and connecting with a chronic pain specialist and psychiatrist. This pain isn’t explained by a single disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So you’re saying it’s in my head?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the pain is real. But it may involve multiple systems—nerves, gut, mental health. A team approach gives you the best chance for improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You’ve passed gas, moved your bowels, and your vitals are stable. We can discharge you if you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m ready. What do I do if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.text: Try Emend first. If that doesn’t help, call your PCP or go to the ER. But try to avoid frequent ER visits if possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and follow up with your doctors. We’re here if something new comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I just hope I can get some relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We all want that for you. This plan is about long-term control, not just crisis management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’m willing to try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best step forward. We’ll get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call us if you need anything before your follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I appreciate it.

conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. In the ER, they gave you fluids, Zofran for nausea, and Dilaudid for pain. Your labs show your hemoglobin dropped a bit since your last admission, but it’s stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was supposed to have a parotid gland biopsy to check for Sjogren’s, but I canceled. My PCP said I should be off methotrexate and Plaquenil for a month first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Actually, we checked with rheumatology and your PCP—only one week off those meds is needed. So you can schedule the biopsy sooner. It’s important to confirm or rule out Sjogren’s, especially with your family history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t know that. I’ll call my PCP. I also haven’t started with the pain clinic or psychiatry yet. My PCP said they’d help set that up.

conversation_lines.text: I know, but my clinic can’t access my Port-a-cath after hours. That’s why I end up here—I can’t get pain relief at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. So I can go home if I keep down food?

conversation_lines.text: Great. I’ll eat slowly and let you know how I feel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve tolerated the meal well. I’ve reviewed your discharge plan. You’re cleared to go home. Here’s your medication list and follow-up instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ll follow up with my team and keep working on this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You’re here because you’ve been vomiting blood. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had two episodes of vomiting blood in the last two days. It’s scary. I was just feeling better after my last hospital stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. You mentioned at the ER that you were recently diagnosed with lupus and started on steroids. Can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, at the other hospital they said my blood work suggested lupus, gave me IV steroids for five days, and sent me home on prednisone. I was feeling great until two days ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And you’ve also had chronic abdominal pain and nausea for years. Did the prednisone help with that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It did, actually. For the first time in months, I wasn’t in pain. But now it’s back—same pain, nausea, and then the vomiting with blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. We’ve checked your labs. Your hemoglobin is low at 10.7, but it’s stable. White blood cells are high, likely from the steroids. No sign of infection in your blood culture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the blood in my vomit from an ulcer again? I had ulcers found on an EGD last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a possibility. We’ll schedule an EGD tomorrow to look inside. For now, we’re giving you IV fluids and continuing your prednisone. We’ve also restarted your Nexium to protect your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also have this cold—sore throat, runny nose. I was on Augmentin, but it made me nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw you were on antibiotics. Since your symptoms are mild and it’s likely a viral URI, we’ll stop the Augmentin. We don’t want to irritate your stomach more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still nauseous, and I had another episode of vomiting, but no blood this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good—no fresh bleeding. Your labs are stable. We’re going to do the EGD today to check for ulcers or other causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they put me to sleep for it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll be sedated. It’s routine. They’ll also take a small biopsy from your duodenum, since you have a history of malabsorption.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back from the EGD. The good news is no active bleeding. They saw a small hiatal hernia and some atrophy in the duodenum. Biopsies were taken.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No ulcers? But I had them before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No new ulcers. The previous ones may have healed. The bleeding might be from a small tear in the esophagus from vomiting—called a Mallory-Weiss tear. It often stops on its own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I’ve heard of that. So it’s not serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not usually. Since your hemoglobin isn’t dropping, we’ll monitor you and keep you on stomach-protecting meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You tolerated a soft diet yesterday without vomiting. How’s your pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Still there, but not as bad. I’m glad I could eat something.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We did an abdominal X-ray yesterday. No blockage, but there’s a lot of stool in your colon. That could be contributing to your discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been constipated since the pain started. I’m not moving much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start a gentle laxative—senna—and docusate to help. Staying regular will help your gut feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your rheumatology workup came back. Most markers are normal. No clear evidence of active lupus here, but we’ll continue your prednisone as started.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But the other doctor said I have lupus. I’m confused.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s confusing. Sometimes diagnoses are made based on symptoms and limited tests. Here, your ANA and other markers are normal. But since you were started on treatment, we don’t stop it abruptly. Your PCP will help decide next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll follow up with her.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. No more vomiting, pain is controlled. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue prednisone, but at a lower dose—20 mg daily. We’re switching from 60 mg. Don’t stop it suddenly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know, I’ve been on it before. What about the stomach medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll stay on esomeprazole twice daily. We’re also adding sucralfate four times a day to coat and protect your stomach lining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And for nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you Zofran tablets that dissolve under the tongue. Use them as needed for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I like those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also adjusting your amitriptyline—from 50 mg to 25 mg at bedtime. It may help with pain and sleep but with fewer side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ve had dry mouth on it before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This dose might help. And keep taking your fludrocortisone and betaxolol for POTS.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had dizziness, so that’s good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Your condition is stable. No active bleeding, pain is manageable, and you’re eating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was worried about the bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. The EGD was reassuring. Keep taking your meds, especially the prednisone. Follow up with your PCP within a week to discuss continuing cellcept if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll call for my biopsy results from the EGD?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your GI doctor will contact you about those. If you vomit blood again, go to the ER. Otherwise, you’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I be worried about Sjogren’s? I was told I might have it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned a positive tear test and salivary issues as a child. But no biopsy was done. Your PCP may want to pursue that, especially with your family history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my dad’s side has lupus and Sjogren’s. I’ll bring it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good idea. For now, focus on recovery. You’ve been through a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your discharge instructions and prescriptions. You can leave once that’s done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy. Rest, stay hydrated, and follow up as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope the prednisone keeps helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should, but your doctor will monitor for side effects and decide if long-term treatment is needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’ll let the nurse know you’re ready for discharge paperwork.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ve been reviewing why you came in. You had three episodes of vomiting blood last night, is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I woke up with this fullness in my stomach and then vomited a cup of blood. Then twice more—each time about a cup. I felt dizzy after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You also mentioned sharp pain in your upper belly that goes to your back. How bad is it now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s throbbing, still pretty bad. I’ve been on Dilaudid at home, but it’s not helping as much as usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you fluids and medication in the ER. Your labs show your hemoglobin dropped a bit, but it’s likely from the fluids diluting your blood, not ongoing bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I *was* bleeding, right? Why can’t we find the source?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did bleed, but your NG tube wash came back clean, and your stool test was negative for blood. Also, you had an EGD just eight days ago—no active bleeding was seen then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what caused it? Could it be my lupus? Or the pancreatitis they used to say I had?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your lupus is being treated with prednisone and methotrexate, which we’ll continue. But imaging hasn’t shown chronic pancreatitis. The bleeding might be from a Mallory-Weiss tear—small tears from vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had so many tests. Why can’t we figure this out? I’m scared it’ll happen again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve done a lot—EGDs, CT scans, capsule endoscopy—all normal except for a small hiatal hernia and some duodenal atrophy. Nothing explains the pain or bleeding clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My mom is worried we’re not doing enough. And you couldn’t find Dr. ___’s recent notes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We see you’ve seen him recently, but his notes aren’t in our system. We’re trying to get them. In the meantime, we’re following your usual meds and monitoring you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been on clear liquids. You vomited apple juice earlier—no blood. That’s a good sign. How’s your pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there. I just want to go home. I can manage my pain meds there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’d prefer you stay a bit longer to make sure you can keep food down and your levels stabilize. But I understand you want to leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do. I’ll follow up with my PCP and Dr. ___. Can I go home now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it’s against medical advice. We recommend bowel rest, advance diet slowly, and return if you vomit blood, can’t keep fluids down, or feel worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I’ll watch for those signs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re sending you home on your usual meds. Prednisone is now 10 mg three times a day. Continue the Nexium and Zofran as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my Dilaudid for pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 2 mg every four hours as needed. Also, we added stool softeners in case the pain meds cause constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll call my doctor tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. If symptoms worsen, go to the ER. We care about your safety, even if you’re leaving AMA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. I just need to be at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve arranged for discharge. A nurse will go over instructions one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Please follow up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I've been reviewing why you came in. You were seen in your rheumatologist’s office today and had a fever and fast heart rate, is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. My heart was up to 140, and I had a low fever—100.4. I also woke up with stomach pain and nausea, which I haven’t had in weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned that since starting the steroid injection three weeks ago, your pain completely went away and you haven’t needed any Dilaudid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. It was amazing—no pain at all. This morning was the first time it came back. I didn’t vomit blood, just clear stuff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. In the ER, they gave you fluids, which brought your heart rate down to the 100s. That’s still a bit high, but I see you have POTS—postural tachycardia—so this might be your normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my heart is usually in the 110s when I’m resting. It jumps when I stand. I take betaxolol, midodrine, and Florinef for it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’ll keep those going. Your labs came back—white blood cell count is normal, lipase is normal, so no sign of pancreatitis flare. Liver tests are fine too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my pancreas again? I’ve had so many scans over the years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing suggests that. Given your history and the fact that you’re on immunosuppressants for lupus, we wanted to check for infection. But you’ve been fever-free since the ER, and you don’t have cough, sore throat, or other signs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do have lupus—diagnosed a few months ago. I get methotrexate and a steroid shot weekly. Did they give me my meds here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held the methotrexate while you're in the hospital, just to be safe with the fever. But you’ll resume it after discharge. The steroid shot is due soon—we’ll make sure you get it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My stomach pain is much better now. I had some Dilaudid in the ER, and the nausea is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep the Zofran available if nausea returns. You can eat regular food if you tolerate it. We also switched your Nexium to pantoprazole—same type of medication, just hospital formulary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. But honestly, I’m feeling pretty well. Can I go home tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve done all the necessary checks—no infection signs, no abdominal emergency. Your urine test was contaminated, so we can’t use it, but you have no urinary symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I really don’t want to stay. I was just worried about the fever and fast heart rate, but now I feel okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright. Since your exam and labs are reassuring, and you’re pain-free now, we can discharge you. We’ll send you home with your regular medications and instructions to follow up with your rheumatologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. Should I worry if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might be related to the lupus or a mild viral issue. Keep taking your meds as prescribed. If you develop high fever, vomiting, or severe pain, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my POTS meds—should I keep those the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue betaxolol, Florinef, and midodrine as before. We adjusted the betaxolol dose slightly—now 10 mg twice daily instead of 20 mg once. It’s the same total amount, just split.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my Lexapro and amitriptyline?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue both. We also kept your Dilaudid for breakthrough pain, but use it sparingly. The goal is to stay off opioids if the steroids are helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I just hope the pain stays away like it did before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor that. Your rheumatologist should help fine-tune your lupus treatment. For now, you’re cleared to go home. I’ll have the nurse bring your discharge papers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I appreciate you listening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care, and don’t hesitate to reach out if things change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you’re still feeling stable and ready for discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I feel fine. Ready to go home.
